title: type aliases versus interfaces — when to use each
hook: Both `type` and `interface` name object shapes in TypeScript, but they behave differently with unions, declaration merging, and extension. Knowing when to pick each is a staple senior interview question.

sections.heading: What are type aliases and interfaces?

blocks.text: A **`type` alias** creates a new name for any type — primitives, unions, intersections, tuples, or objects. An **`interface`** declares the shape of an object and supports **declaration merging** (multiple declarations with the same name combine). Both can describe object shapes, but only `type` can express unions (`A | B`), mapped types, and conditional types. Interfaces can `extend` other interfaces and classes can `implement` them.

entries.plainDefinition: A name for any TypeScript type expression using the `type` keyword.
A contract for object shape. Supports extends and declaration merging.
When two declarations with the same interface name are combined into one type.
TypeScript checks shape, not declaration name. If it has the properties, it fits.
entries.example: `{ x: 1 }` is assignable to `{ x: number }`

blocks.text: Teams argue about `type` vs `interface` endlessly. The practical answer: use **interface** for public object contracts (especially libraries and `.d.ts` augmentation). Use **type** for unions, intersections, primitives, tuples, and utility-type compositions. C# has `interface` for contracts and `class` for implementation — TypeScript interfaces have no run-time presence, similar to C# interfaces before run-time type info.

blocks.title: Decision guide
blocks.body: Object shape for a class or API surface → `interface`. Union, tuple, mapped type, or primitive alias → `type`. Need declaration merging → `interface`. Everything else → `type`.

sections.heading: How it works step by step

items.title: Object-only shape, may be extended
items.body: Prefer `interface User { ... }` — clearer intent, supports `extends`, classes can `implement`.

items.title: Augmenting third-party types
items.body: Use `interface` in a `.d.ts` file — declaration merging adds properties to existing types.

items.title: Performance note
items.body: For very large codebases, interfaces are slightly faster for the compiler to check on extends chains. Negligible for most projects.

diagram.title: type vs interface decision tree

snippet.label: interface for object contracts
snippet.explanation: Lines 1–5: `interface` describes an object shape with an optional property. Lines 7–9: `extends` adds fields. Lines 11–14: classes `implement` interfaces — compile-time check only, no run-time enforcement.

snippet.label: type for unions and primitives
snippet.explanation: Line 1: primitive union — only `type` can do this. Lines 3–5: discriminated union for API results. Line 7: tuple alias. Line 9: utility type composition — requires `type`.

snippet.label: Declaration merging with interface
snippet.explanation: Lines 2–4 and 7–9: two `interface Window` declarations merge into one. This is impossible with `type` — duplicate type aliases are an error. Essential for augmenting global objects and library types.

blocks.title: Pitfalls to avoid
blocks.body: Using `interface` for unions (syntax error). Expecting interfaces to enforce run-time shape (they are compile-time only). Over-using declaration merging in application code (reserve for `.d.ts` augmentation). Declaring `type Foo = { ... }` and `interface Foo` with the same name in the same scope.

blocks.text: TypeScript uses structural typing — two interfaces with the same shape are interchangeable regardless of name. C# uses nominal typing for classes (name matters) but interfaces are also nominally checked. `interface` extends create a single flat type; `type` intersections can produce impossible combinations (conflicting property types). For library authors, prefer `interface` for public API surfaces so consumers can augment. For application code, team lint rules (e.g. `@typescript-eslint/consistent-type-definitions`) settle the debate.

blocks.title: What gets you rejected in interviews
blocks.body: Saying they are completely identical. Not knowing declaration merging exists. Claiming interfaces exist at run time. Unable to explain when you must use type (unions).

interviewTakeaways: type for unions, tuples, primitives, and utility compositions.
interface for object shapes, extends, class implements, and declaration merging.
Both are erased at run time — no run-time enforcement.
60s: type for unions and complex types. interface for object contracts and merging. Structural typing — shape matters, not name.
Follow-up: what is declaration merging and when would you use it?
commonPitfalls: Claiming interface and type are always interchangeable.
Using interface for unions — syntax error.
Strong answer: 'type for unions/tuples/mapped types. interface for object contracts and .d.ts augmentation. Both compile away.'

jsTsCorrelations.note: JavaScript has no interface keyword. JSDoc `@typedef` is the closest analogue for documenting object shapes without TypeScript.
C# interfaces are nominal and exist at run time via reflection. TypeScript interfaces are structural and erased — only the shape matters.
